narrative:
The model predicted an 85.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this probability is quite high, your application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily against you were your class ranking in your third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you at the very bottom of your class (decile 1 versus an average of about 6 among accepted students). This was the single most influential piece of information and strongly signaled higher risk of failing the bar. Your LSAT score of 22 was also far below the average of 37 seen among accepted applicants, giving the model another clear reason to expect difficulty passing the bar. Finally, your first-year ranking (again decile 1 versus an average around 6) added further weight in the same negative direction.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 (versus 3.23 average) and middle family income also pointed in the same direction, though they played smaller roles. The fact that you plan to attend full-time was actually slightly positive, but not enough to offset the other signals.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance dramatically in the remaining law school years, consider retaking the LSAT if possible, and look for structured bar-prep support programs. These steps can meaningfully change the picture for future applications or for passing the bar itself. (248 words)
